reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Presents as sudden, painless, profound loss of vision in one eye, often to counting fingers or worse
A relative afferent pupillary defect is present in the affected eye
Fundoscopy shows a pale, oedematous retina with a classic cherry-red spot at the fovea and attenuated, segmented ('cattle-trucking') arterioles
It is effectively a stroke of the eye — treat as a time-critical emergency and investigate the same as an acute cerebral ischaemic event
Always exclude giant cell arteritis in older patients by asking about jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and headache and checking inflammatory markers
Immediate measures aim to dislodge or reperfuse (ocular massage, lowering intraocular pressure), though evidence for benefit is limited once the window has passed
Urgent referral for stroke workup (carotid imaging, cardiac source, vascular risk factors) is essential to prevent a subsequent cerebral stroke
reference.pathophysiology: Central retinal artery occlusion results from acute interruption of blood flow in the central retinal artery, most often from an embolus (carotid or cardiac) or from thrombosis, arteritis, or vasospasm. The inner retina, supplied by this artery, is exquisitely sensitive to ischaemia; sudden occlusion causes rapid infarction and oedema of the inner retinal layers. The fovea, supplied by the underlying choroid, retains its colour and stands out as a cherry-red spot against the surrounding pale, opaque ischaemic retina. Irreversible neuronal damage occurs within a short ischaemic window.
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundoscopy for retinal pallor and cherry-red spot
Assessment for a relative afferent pupillary defect
ESR, CRP, and platelets to screen for giant cell arteritis, with temporal artery biopsy if suspected
Carotid Doppler ultrasound to identify an embolic source
Cardiac evaluation including ECG and echocardiography
Blood pressure, glucose, and lipid assessment; OCT and fluorescein angiography as adjuncts
redFlags: Time-critical emergency — inner retinal infarction becomes irreversible within a short window, so treat and refer immediately
Suspected giant cell arteritis threatens the fellow eye and requires urgent systemic treatment without waiting for biopsy
It is a warning of systemic embolic disease with high risk of subsequent cerebral stroke
Bilateral or ophthalmic artery involvement suggesting a major vascular or arteritic process
reference.prognosis: Visual prognosis is generally poor, with permanent severe visual loss common; the main priority becomes preventing a devastating cerebral stroke and protecting the fellow eye.
pitfalls: Failing to consider and treat giant cell arteritis in an older patient, risking loss of the second eye
Treating it as an isolated eye problem rather than initiating urgent stroke and vascular workup
Dilating or delaying assessment and missing the narrow reperfusion window
Confusing it with vein occlusion, which shows haemorrhages rather than retinal pallor
management: Treat as a stroke of the eye with emergency referral and the same acute pathway and workup as cerebral ischaemia
Immediate reperfusion attempts within the ischaemic window using ocular massage and measures to lower intraocular pressure such as anterior chamber paracentesis and pressure-lowering drugs
Urgent exclusion and treatment of giant cell arteritis with high-dose corticosteroids when suspected in older patients
Secondary prevention with antiplatelet therapy and control of hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidaemia
Carotid and cardiac evaluation for an embolic source with directed treatment such as carotid endarterectomy or anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation
Stroke or transient ischaemic attack service referral with neuroimaging
Low-vision support and monitoring and protection of the fellow eye
